reason: The sources provide enough multi-verified facts to support a surprising 45-second space story.
story: Discovered in 1877, Stephan's Quintet in Pegasus looks like a tight squad of five interacting galaxies. But space is full of photobombers. Modern telescopes revealed that one of them, NGC 7320, is actually a foreground interloper sitting just thirty-nine million light-years away, while the other four are parked a staggering three hundred million light-years out. To make matters crazier, another intruder named NGC 7318B is currently plowing straight into the group at millions of miles per hour. This supersonic impact generates a colossal shock wave bigger than the entire Milky Way, tearing apart gas clouds and triggering frantic bursts of star birth. Even Hollywood got in on the act, using an old image of the quintet to represent glowing angels in the 1946 holiday classic It's a Wonderful Life.
angle: A galaxy in Stephan's Quintet is actually a close-up foreground interloper, while another is plowing through the group at supersonic speeds, creating a shockwave bigger than the Milky Way.

claims.claim: Stephan's Quintet was discovered in 1877 by Édouard Stephan.
The group is located in the constellation Pegasus.
Four of the five galaxies form a true physical association known as Hickson Compact Group 92.
The brightest member and visual grouping non-member, NGC 7320, is located about 39 million light-years from Earth.
The other four main galaxies are about 210 to 340 million light-years away.
NGC 7318B is falling into the center of the group at supersonic speeds of several million kilometers per hour.
The collision generates an immense shock wave bigger than the Milky Way.
Images of Stephan's Quintet were used to represent talking or angelic figures at the beginning of the 1946 holiday film It's a Wonderful Life.
NASA's James Webb Space Telescope selected Stephan's Quintet as one of its first official science image targets in 2022.
NASA's Spitzer Space Telescope discovered a very powerful molecular hydrogen signal from the shock wave.
The Chandra X-ray Observatory detected gas heated to millions of degrees emitting X-rays from the shock region.
NGC 7319 contains a type 2 Seyfert active galactic nucleus.

disputed: Whether NGC 7320C or other past visitors passed through the center multiple times is treated as an interpretation or belief by some accounts and should be attributed if mentioned.
